# Lessons from Part II {.unnumbered}

Seven data structures in seven chapters, and the surprise — to me, at least, the second time I taught this material — is how *few atoms* the whole part is built from. Two layout choices (contiguous and linked), one function (hash), and a small collection of disciplines about which operations to make cheap. That's it. The dynamic array and the linked list are the atoms. The stack, queue, deque, hash table, Bloom filter, and union-find are *compositions* of those atoms with restrictions or extensions imposed on top.

I want to spend this short closing essay doing two things. First, naming the patterns that kept showing up across the seven chapters — the ones the chapters themselves only had time to gesture at. Second, identifying the bridge into Part III, where the structures get hierarchical and the moves you learned here get a new dimension to operate in.

## The patterns that kept showing up

**The operation-versus-layout trade.** Every chapter was, at its core, an answer to "which operations do I want to be cheap, and what am I willing to give up to get there?" Chapter 8 made indexed access cheap and prepend expensive. Chapter 9 made cheap surgery in the middle and indexed access expensive. Chapter 10 took an array (or a chain) and restricted operations to one end. Chapter 12 made point lookup cheap by abandoning key order. Chapter 13 made point lookup cheap by *abandoning the keys themselves*. The trade isn't a footnote; it's the whole story. There is no single best sequence data structure, because the right answer depends on which operations the caller actually exercises.

**Amortization as the analytical move.** The accountant's view of cost — *what does this operation cost on average, over many calls, rather than in the worst case?* — appeared three times. Chapter 8 introduced it on the doubling dynamic array. Chapter 12 inherited it on hash-table rehashing. Chapter 14 pushed it to its most striking conclusion on union-find, where amortized analysis was the only way to express the inverse-Ackermann bound at all. The pattern in each case was the same: rare, expensive, self-modifying operations subsidized by many cheap operations. Doubling-and-copy in the dynamic array. Doubling-and-rehash in the hash table. Path-compression flattening in union-find. Same accountant, three different ledgers.

**Discipline-as-restriction as a design tool.** Stacks and queues aren't new data structures — they're arrays (or linked lists) with most of the operations turned off. The act of *removing* operations is the value, because it lets you reason about an algorithm's order of operations without tracking the sequence's contents. Function calls work because the language *forbids* you from reaching past the top of the stack. Breadth-first search works because the FIFO discipline *guarantees* you process the closest unvisited nodes first. The same move underlies union-find — a partition with the only operations being "merge" and "ask which piece this element is in" — and the same move shows up in Part III (priority queues, where the only operations are insert and remove-min), Part IV (suffix arrays, where the only operations are query by prefix), and Part V (graph representations, where the only operations are "iterate neighbors"). Restriction is what makes a data structure *be about something* rather than just hold data.

**Escaping the comparison model.** Hash tables and Bloom filters both win by *not comparing* keys. They compute on key content, treat the result as an address, and skip the comparison-tree lower bound entirely. The same move underlies counting and radix sort from chapter 6 of Part I, and it returns in Part IV (rolling hashes for pattern matching), Part VIII (modular-arithmetic-based primality testing), and Part IX (probabilistic data structures — Count-Min sketch, HyperLogLog, all extensions of the Bloom filter's "compute on content, store the fingerprint" pattern). The deeper lesson: a *lower bound is a property of a model, not a property of a problem* — exactly the lesson Part I closed on, applied again in a new costume.

**Trading exactness for space.** Bloom filters and the monotonic deque are both versions of the same move: identify exactly what the workload needs to know, and design a structure that stores only *that*, with a known error rate or known approximation tolerance on the side that's allowed to be inexact. The Bloom filter stores membership without the keys. The monotonic deque stores only the currently-undominated candidates for being the window maximum. Both are *information-preserving for the operation that matters and information-discarding for everything else*. The pattern recurs in Part IX with the streaming and probabilistic structures, and it shows up in Part VIII when geometric algorithms summarize point sets with their convex hulls.

**Composition by small atoms.** The Part II structures stack on each other in a very literal way. Chapter 9's `Node[T]` shows up inside chapter 10's `LinkedStack` and chapter 11's `LinkedQueue`. Chapter 9's `DoublyLinkedNode[T]` is the backbone of chapter 11's `Deque`. Chapter 12's chained hash map uses the same chain-with-pointer-surgery idiom as chapter 9's linked list. Chapter 13's Bloom filter uses chapter 12's double-hashing trick to simulate $k$ independent hashes. Chapter 14's union-find array layout is the same dense-array pattern as chapter 8's dynamic array. Nothing in Part II is built from scratch; everything builds on what came before.

## What I want you to take with you

Five meta-lessons survive the specifics. None of them are new with this book; all of them are easier to articulate after a part that exercises them deliberately.

**1. A data structure is a *contract*, not an implementation.** The stack contract is push-pop-peek. Two implementations satisfy it — array-backed and linked-backed — and any caller that depends only on the contract can swap them freely. The same is true of every structure in this part. Designing software around the contract rather than the implementation is what makes refactors possible decades later, and it's what makes the structures in the rest of the book composable.

**2. Memory layout is not an implementation detail.** The single decision between contiguous and linked storage dictates which operations are cheap, which are expensive, and which are simply impossible. Choosing the layout is doing real algorithmic work. In a language like C or Rust where you control the layout explicitly, this is obvious. In a language like Python where most layout decisions are hidden behind built-in types, it's easy to forget — and easy to choose the wrong structure because the wrong one was the default. Cache locality, allocator behavior, and pointer overhead are not separate from algorithm design; they're part of it.

**3. The right error guarantee is sometimes one-sided.** Bloom filters are useful precisely because their wrongness is asymmetric — they're never wrong about negatives, only about positives. That asymmetric contract is what lets them be used as a pre-filter without compromising the overall system's correctness. The same shape shows up in caches (always wrong toward "stale" but never toward "fabricated"), in sketches that approximate from below but never above, and in security protocols where false positives are recoverable but false negatives are catastrophic. The design question isn't always "be exact"; sometimes it's "be wrong in *this specific direction* with *this specific bound*."

**4. Amortized analysis is how data structures actually live.** Real workloads don't exercise worst cases on every operation; they exercise the *distribution* of operations, and the structure's cost is the integral over that distribution. The doubling dynamic array is the cleanest example, but the same accounting underlies every modern data structure that does any kind of internal reorganization — LRU caches, B-trees, persistent functional structures, the JIT compilation tier in a runtime. Worst-case analysis is what lets you reason about a single operation in isolation. Amortized analysis is what lets you reason about the *system*.

**5. Composition over selection.** No one in production picks "the" data structure. Hash tables are built on dynamic arrays. Heaps are built on dynamic arrays. LRU caches combine hash tables with doubly linked lists. Tries are trees of hash tables. Production sorting routines combine multiple sorts. The skill the rest of the book is going to keep exercising isn't "remember which structure goes with which problem" — it's *compose the right structure for this specific workload from the atoms you have available*. The Part II atoms are the ones you'll keep reaching for, throughout the rest of the book and out into every real codebase you'll ever work in.

## What's next

Part III is another change of altitude. The seven structures in this part were *flat* — sequences, partitions, sets, with no hierarchical organization in their layout. The next eight chapters introduce *trees*: hierarchical data structures where each element has a parent (sometimes several children, sometimes a single linear chain that happens to branch). Trees are how you get $\Theta(\log n)$ operations on ordered data, which is the cost shape that sits between Part I's $\Theta(n)$ and Part II's $\Theta(1)$, and which turns out to be exactly the right cost for most real-world sorted-data workloads where range queries matter.

The Part II atoms keep paying out in Part III. Trees are built from linked nodes (chapter 9). Balanced trees use rotations that look a lot like chapter 9's pointer surgery, scaled up to a hierarchical context. Heaps are built on dynamic arrays (chapter 8) with implicit parent-child pointers. Tries hash characters into child arrays (chapter 12). Segment trees and Fenwick trees use the dense-array-with-implicit-pointers trick that union-find pioneered (chapter 14). You won't be relearning these atoms — you'll be watching them get arranged into branching shapes that unlock a new set of operations the flat structures couldn't support.

Seven chapters, seven structures, one part. The atoms are small. The compositions are everywhere. Onward.
